title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
authors: Edward J. Hu, Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li, Shean Wang, Lu Wang, Weizhu Chen

pages.title: Freeze the big model, train tiny low-rank adapters

blocks.html: The problem. The standard way to specialize a large language model for your task is full fine-tuning: take all of the model's parameters and keep training them on your data. For GPT-3 that means updating all 175 billion numbers. Every task you care about then needs its own 175B-parameter copy. Storing one such checkpoint takes about 350GB; storing ten takes 3.5TB. And during training you also need memory for the optimizer state — Adam keeps two extra numbers (a running mean and variance of the gradient) per parameter — so the working memory is roughly triple the size of the model itself.

The intuition. Imagine you bought a fully-equipped car and you only want to change how it handles on one specific road. You would not rebuild the whole engine — you would add a small tuning module. LoRA does exactly this for neural networks: it freezes the giant pre-trained model and bolts on a small, trainable add-on for each weight matrix you want to influence.

The mechanism in one line. For a weight matrix $W$ that full fine-tuning would have changed to $W + \Delta W$, LoRA does not store the full change $\Delta W$. Instead it writes the change as a product of two skinny matrices, $\Delta W = BA$, where $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$ and $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$, and $r$ (the rank) is tiny — often 1, 2, 4, or 8. Only $A$ and $B$ are trained; $W$ never moves.

blocks.tex: h = W x + \Delta W x = W x + B A x

blocks.html: Reading this term by term: $x \in \mathbb{R}^{k}$ is the input vector to the layer; $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$ is the frozen pre-trained weight that maps a $k$-dimensional input to a $d$-dimensional output; $h \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ is the layer output. $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$ first squeezes the input down to a tiny $r$-dimensional bottleneck, and $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$ expands it back up to the $d$-dimensional output space. The two paths ($Wx$ and $BAx$) are simply added.
LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000x and the GPU memory requirement by 3x, while performing on par or better than fine-tuning on RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2, and GPT-3.

Concrete payoff. For GPT-3 175B, trainable parameters drop from 175,000,000,000 to about 4,700,000 — roughly a 10,000x reduction. The per-task checkpoint shrinks from 350GB to about 35MB (small enough to email). And because $BA$ can be folded back into $W$ before deployment, there is zero extra inference latency.

Why this is in the collection. LoRA is now the default parameter-efficient fine-tuning method across the open-source world (it is the core of HuggingFace's PEFT library). It made the next paper, QLoRA, possible, and it underpins the explosion of community fine-tunes that followed.

pages.title: Why full fine-tuning hurts at scale

blocks.html: The question this page answers: if fine-tuning already works, what exactly is wrong with it? The answer is operational cost, and it gets worse the bigger the base model is.

A concrete scenario. Suppose you run a SaaS product and want a customized model for each of your 1,000 enterprise customers. With full fine-tuning of a 175B model, you would need 1,000 separate 350GB checkpoints — 350TB of storage just for weights, plus the engineering nightmare of loading a fresh 350GB model into GPU memory every time a different customer's request comes in. Hot-swapping is impossible at that size.

items: Storage: one full checkpoint per task, each the size of the entire model.
Training memory: weights + gradients + Adam's two moment buffers ≈ 3-4x the model size in VRAM.
Deployment: you cannot keep many full models warm; switching tasks means reloading hundreds of GB.

blocks.html: Prior attempts and why they fell short. Two earlier parameter-efficient approaches are the obvious predecessors:

items: Adapter layers (Houlsby et al., 2019): insert small new bottleneck layers between the frozen Transformer layers. They train few parameters, but because the adapters run sequentially in the forward pass, they add real inference latency — a problem when you serve at low batch size, as in interactive use.

Prefix tuning (Li & Liang, 2021): prepend trainable 'virtual tokens' to the input. It works but is finicky to optimize, and the virtual tokens eat into the usable context length, leaving less room for the actual prompt.

blocks.html: LoRA's design goal was to get adapter-level parameter savings with zero added latency and without stealing context length.
The core bet. LoRA is built on an empirical observation: although a model has billions of weights, the change needed to adapt it to a new task lives in a surprisingly small subspace.

An analogy. Think of a 1,000-page reference manual (the pre-trained model). To make it useful for a specific job, you do not rewrite it — you add a one-page sticky note of corrections and emphases. The note is low-dimensional relative to the manual. LoRA claims $\Delta W$ is that sticky note.

The evidence it builds on. Aghajanyan et al. (2020) measured the intrinsic dimension of fine-tuning — the smallest number of free parameters you can optimize in a random low-dimensional subspace and still reach good task performance. They found it is shockingly low (often a few hundred to a few thousand) even for models with hundreds of millions of weights.

The leap. If the update is intrinsically low-rank, then don't discover that structure by accident — bake it into the parameterization. Writing $\Delta W = BA$ with rank $r$ forces the update to be at most rank $r$ by construction. The hypothesis is restated formally in the method: the rank of the adaptation $\Delta W$ can be very low and still match full fine-tuning.
The setup. For a frozen pre-trained weight $W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$, LoRA writes the adapted weight as:

blocks.tex: W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + B A, \quad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r},\; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k},\; r \ll \min(d, k)

blocks.html: Term by term: $W_0$ is the frozen base matrix (no gradient ever flows to it). $\Delta W = BA$ is the trainable update. $B$ has $d \cdot r$ entries; $A$ has $r \cdot k$ entries; together $r(d+k)$ trainable numbers, versus $d \cdot k$ for a full update. The constraint $r \ll \min(d,k)$ is what makes the saving huge.

A worked count. Take a GPT-3 attention projection with $d = k = 12{,}288$. A full $\Delta W$ has $12{,}288 \times 12{,}288 \approx 151$ million entries. With $r = 8$, LoRA needs only $8 \times (12{,}288 + 12{,}288) \approx 196{,}608$ entries — about 0.13% of the full update, a 768x reduction for this single matrix.
The forward pass becomes the sum of the frozen path and the adapter path:

blocks.tex: h = W_0 x + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A x

blocks.html: Here $\alpha$ is a constant scaling hyperparameter and $r$ the rank. The factor $\frac{\alpha}{r}$ scales the adapter's contribution. Why divide by $r$? So that if you later change the rank, you do not also accidentally change the typical magnitude of the update — the scaling keeps $\Delta W$ roughly the same size whether $r=4$ or $r=64$, which means you do not have to re-tune the learning rate every time you change $r$. In practice you set $\alpha$ once (e.g. $\alpha = 16$) and treat $\alpha/r$ like a fixed gain.

Initialization is the clever part. $A$ is initialized with small random Gaussian values; $B$ is initialized to all zeros. Therefore at step 0, $\Delta W = B A = 0$, so the model is byte-for-byte identical to the pre-trained base. Training starts exactly at the strong pre-trained solution and can only move away as $B$ learns — there is no random-init shock that could damage the model's existing knowledge.

Why zero $B$ and not zero $A$? If both were zero, no gradient could flow (the product and its derivatives would all be zero). With random $A$ and zero $B$, the gradient with respect to $B$ is nonzero on the first step, so learning can begin immediately while still starting from $\Delta W = 0$.

pages.title: Which weights to adapt, and the no-latency trick

blocks.html: The question. A Transformer has many weight matrices. In each attention block there are four projections — query $W_q$, key $W_k$, value $W_v$, output $W_o$ — plus two large feed-forward matrices. Where should the limited LoRA budget go?

The empirical answer. Under a fixed parameter budget, adapting just the query and value projections, $W_q$ and $W_v$, gives the best quality. The paper's ablation on GPT-3 shows that, given the same total number of trainable parameters, spreading rank across $\{W_q, W_v\}$ beats putting it all into $W_q$ alone or adding $W_k$.
The lesson: it is better to adapt more matrices at lower rank than one matrix at high rank. A tiny rank (even $r=1$ or $r=2$) spread across the attention is enough.

The no-latency trick — the headline practical advantage. Adapters add latency because they are extra layers. LoRA does not, because $\Delta W = BA$ has the exact same shape as $W_0$. After training, you compute once:

and store $W$ as a single matrix. The deployed model is structurally identical to the original — same number of matmuls, same shapes — so inference is exactly as fast as the base model. If you need to serve many tasks, you keep $W_0$ shared and the small $(A,B)$ pairs separate, swapping them in microseconds; if you serve one task, you merge and pay nothing.

What was tested. LoRA is benchmarked against full fine-tuning, several adapter variants, prefix tuning, and BitFit, across RoBERTa-base/large, DeBERTa-XXL (1.5B), GPT-2 medium/large, and GPT-3 175B. Tasks span GLUE (a suite of language-understanding tasks), WikiSQL (text-to-SQL), MNLI (natural language inference), SAMSum (dialogue summarization), and E2E NLG (data-to-text generation).

items: RoBERTa-large on GLUE: LoRA with 0.8M trainable params matches the GLUE average of full fine-tuning, which trains all 355M params — a ~440x reduction at equal quality.
GPT-3 175B on WikiSQL: LoRA with 4.7M trainable params reaches 73.4% accuracy, statistically tied with full fine-tuning (73.8%), while prefix-based methods trail by 2-4 points.

GPT-3 175B on MNLI-matched: LoRA scores 91.7% versus full fine-tuning's 89.5% — LoRA actually beats full fine-tuning, plausibly because constraining the update to low rank acts as a regularizer and prevents overfitting the relatively small task data.

blocks.html: Why beating full fine-tuning is not a paradox. Full fine-tuning has enough capacity to memorize quirks of the training set. The low-rank constraint is a strong prior that the adaptation should be simple; on tasks where the true adaptation really is simple, that prior helps generalization, the same way a smaller model can sometimes generalize better than a larger over-parameterized one.

pages.title: Why it works: anatomy of the low-rank update

blocks.html: The question. Section 7 of the paper asks: what is the update $\Delta W$ actually doing to the model? Three findings stand out.

items: Rank can be tiny. Even $r = 1$ or $r = 2$ captures most of the task signal; going beyond $r = 8$ rarely helps. This is direct confirmation of the low-intrinsic-rank hypothesis.

The update amplifies under-used directions. When the authors compare the subspace of $\Delta W$ to the top singular directions of $W$, they find $\Delta W$ does not just reinforce what $W$ already emphasizes. Instead it amplifies feature directions that were present in $W$ but had small magnitude — task-relevant signals the pre-trained model knew about but under-weighted.
The amplification is large. The features $\Delta W$ emphasizes are scaled up by roughly 20x relative to their weak presence in $W_0$ — a small, sharp, targeted nudge rather than a broad rotation.

blocks.html: The takeaway. Fine-tuning a big model for a new task is mostly about turning up the volume on a handful of latent features the model already represents, not teaching it fundamentally new structure. That is precisely the kind of change a low-rank matrix can express, which is why LoRA loses nothing.
The lasting impact. LoRA became the default parameter-efficient fine-tuning method almost immediately because it wins on every axis that matters operationally:

items: Composable: multiple LoRAs can be summed to blend tasks or styles, and a single base can host a marketplace of swappable adapters (the entire 'LoRA' ecosystem in image generation works this way).
Cheap to store and switch: a 7B base plus ten 30MB adapters is ~14.3GB instead of ten 14GB copies (~140GB).
No quality penalty in most regimes, and occasionally a gain from the regularization effect.

blocks.html: The bridge to the next paper. LoRA still requires the frozen base to sit in GPU memory in full precision (fp16) during fine-tuning — for a 65B model that is ~130GB, beyond a single GPU. QLoRA (the next entry) removes that last barrier by quantizing the frozen base to 4-bit, so a 65B model can be fine-tuned on one 48GB GPU. LoRA is the trainable part; QLoRA shrinks the frozen part underneath it.
